synopsis: Fault evidence is required alongside intended-function validation: the braking architecture must address sensor, computation, communication and actuator faults, while fault injection alone cannot establish perception performance when hardware works normally [f384, f10528, f659]. MOSH requires supplier FMECA identification of critical faults, fail-to-safe within 500 ms of critical-failure detection, and lost-connection detection within 500 ms [f2358, f2359, f12076]. The recommended allocation is SIL for test volume and HIL for timing, interfaces and faults; ISO 13849-2:2012 includes software simulation of faults, but SIL cannot prove final-ECU timing, processor or I/O faults [f12057, f9767, f5269]. Nominal simulation fidelity does not demonstrate fault tolerance: corrupted messages, dropouts, timing faults, bus congestion, frozen values and actuator faults need explicit testing, and replay cannot establish performance for failures absent from its logs [f8199, f8200, f5241]. Degraded braking, thermal limits and brake-system state belong in the safety case; sensor unavailability differs from confidently incorrect sensing, and recovery or degraded modes can remain unsafe despite successful nominal collision avoidance [f3634, f7464, f10777]. Unnecessary braking dominates the cited on-road failure evidence, although complaints do not always indicate defects; the booklet also identifies omitted brake-degradation questions and warns that postponing fault-response decisions until prototype delivery can consume the four-month validation window [f1223, f1229, f6593, f10540].
